metadata.title: Why Your Track Sounds Thin On A Phone
metadata.note: Audio-concept explainer: mono fold-down, for someone who has never opened an audio editor. Through-line: most people hear one speaker, which forces the two sides to be added, and opposite content adds to nothing. ONE measured number only (−49.5 dB on the wide layer) — see MEASUREMENTS.txt. The comb-filter beat is kept CONCEPTUAL (holes, not silence); the measured frequency table was cut as too technical for this audience. WRITTEN FOR A COMPLETE BEGINNER. Beat 1 is a BACKGROUND beat that starts from what sound even is and shows where the viewer meets this setting; beat 2 leads with an everyday ANALOGY before any mechanism. No jargon survives without a plain-language definition in the same sentence. Balance, not dumbing down: the viewer should finish able to make the decision themselves. WORD-CLOCK CHOREOGRAPHED via cues.json + sync_cues.py — every reveal lands on a measured spoken phrase, never a guessed fraction. TYPOGRAPHY: Source Serif 4 + Inter loaded via @remotion/google-fonts. Earlier reels silently fell back to system Georgia because no scene loaded a font. NAME: narration spells the presenter phonetically as 'Row-Haan'; all ON-SCREEN text keeps the correct spelling 'Rohan V.'.

beats.narration_text: Hi, I'm Row-Haan, for Humanitarians AI. Your track sounds full and wide in your headphones. You send it to a friend, they play it on their phone, and it comes back thin and hollow. Nothing broke. Part of your music is cancelling itself out — and it is completely predictable once you can see it.

props.segment: Why Your Track Sounds Thin On A Phone
props.command: Why does my track sound full in headphones but thin on a phone speaker?
output: stereo means two slightly different sides
one speaker has to add them together
opposite parts add up to nothing

beats.narration_text: Recorded music has two sides: a left and a right. Slightly different from each other, and that difference is what makes music feel wide. Headphones keep them apart — left side to your left ear, right side to your right. But a phone, a laptop, a smart speaker: that is one single speaker. And one speaker cannot play two things at once. It has to add them together first.

props.title: Two Sides, One Speaker
props.sparkLine: One speaker only ever gets the total.

beats.narration_text: Picture two people pushing the same door. Both push the same way and it swings open easily. But if one pushes while the other pulls, just as hard, the door does not move at all. Both of them are working. Nothing happens. Adding two sides together does exactly this. Where they agree, you get sound. Where they are opposite, you get nothing.

So I built a track and measured it. The bass and the vocal, both sitting in the centre, came through untouched — identical before and after. But a wide, airy layer, spread across the two sides, dropped by almost fifty decibels. Effectively gone. What survives one speaker is whatever sits in the middle.

props.title: What Survives, And What Does Not
props.footnote: Measured with ffmpeg on a track built for this: one side alone, then the same track summed to a single speaker.
props.sparkLine: What survives is what sits in the middle.

beats.narration_text: It is rarely that dramatic, though. Most stereo width comes from delaying one side by a fraction of a millisecond — and when that gets added together, only certain frequencies cancel. You don't lose the whole layer. You lose holes out of it. That is why a folded-down mix usually sounds hollow rather than silent.

props.title: Holes, Not Silence
props.sparkLine: Hollow, not silent. That is the tell.

beats.narration_text: The fix costs ten seconds. Before you export, switch your track to mono and listen once. If the vocal jumps forward and the air disappears, you have found it. The usual culprits are stereo wideners, doubled parts, and wide reverb on something that should be sitting in the centre.

props.title: The Ten-Second Check
props.lede: Switch to mono and listen, once.
steps: Play it on one speaker before you export. Your phone will do.
If the vocal jumps forward and the air vanishes, something is cancelling.
Usual culprits: stereo wideners, doubled parts, wide reverb on a centre element.
Keep the bass and the lead voice in the middle — those are what has to survive.
props.sparkLine: Ten seconds, before anyone else hears it.

beats.narration_text: Most people will hear your track on one speaker. Check it there before you call it finished. I'm Row-Haan, for Humanitarians AI.
